items.stem: A point P moves so that it is always 4 cm from a fixed point O.

parts.t: Write down the mathematical name of the locus of P.
Calculate the total length of this locus. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

ms:
B1
‘circle’ alone is enough; ‘circumference’ also accepted
sols: P is always the same distance (4 cm) from the single fixed point O.
The locus is a circle, centre O, radius 4 cm
a constant distance from one fixed point always gives a circle
Length of the locus = circumference = 2πr
= 2 × π × 4 = 8π = 25.132…
Length = 25.1 cm (3 s.f.)
exact value 8π cm

items.stem: The line AB is 8 cm long and has been drawn for you.

parts.t: Using a straight edge and compasses only, construct the locus of the points that are equidistant from A and from B. Leave in all your construction arcs.
Write down the mathematical name of this locus.

ms:
B1 for two pairs of arcs of equal radius, centred on A and on B, meeting above and below AB
B1 for the correct straight line drawn through the two intersections
arcs must be seen (nfww)

B1
‘perpendicular bisector’ oe; must mention both perpendicular and bisector
sols: Open the compasses to more than half of AB and keep that radius fixed.
the radius must be more than 4 cm so that the arcs cross
With the compass point on A, draw arcs above and below AB.
With the same radius and the compass point on B, draw two more arcs crossing the first pair.
Join the two crossing points with a ruler — this is the required locus
every point of that line is the same distance from A as from B
The line passes through the midpoint of AB and meets AB at 90°.
The locus is the perpendicular bisector of AB

parts.t: Using a straight edge and compasses only, construct the bisector of angle PQR. Leave in all your construction arcs.
Write down the size of the angle between QP and this bisector.

ms:
B1 for one arc centred on Q cutting both QP and QR, then two equal arcs from those two points
B1 for the ruled line from Q through the intersection of those arcs
arcs must be seen (nfww)
sols: Put the compass point on Q and draw one arc that crosses both QP and QR. Call these crossings X and Y.
QX = QY, because they are radii of the same arc.
With the compasses open to a fixed radius, draw an arc from X and an equal arc from Y, meeting at a point Z inside the angle.
Join Q to Z with a ruler — this is the bisector of angle PQR
triangles QXZ and QYZ are congruent (SSS), so the two angles at Q are equal
The bisector cuts the 76° angle into two equal parts.
Angle between QP and the bisector = 76 ÷ 2 = 38°

items.stem:
AB is a straight fence of length 12 m in a large field.
A goat is attached to a ring by a rope of length 5 m. The ring can slide along the whole of the fence.
The dashed line in the diagram is the boundary of the region of the field the goat can reach.

parts.t: Show that the perimeter of this boundary is (24 + 10π) m.
Calculate the total area of the field the goat can reach. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

ms:
M1 for 2 × 12 seen for the two straight parts, or 2 × π × 5 seen for the two semicircular ends
A1 nfww
sols: The ring slides along the whole fence, so the boundary has two straight parts, each parallel to AB and 5 m from it.
Straight parts: 2 × 12 = 24 m
each has the same length as the fence
At each end the goat sweeps a semicircle of radius 5 m, centred on A and on B.
Curved parts: 2 × <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>2</sub> × 2 × π × 5 = 10π m
two semicircles make one whole circle of radius 5 m
Perimeter = (24 + 10π) m as required
this is 55.4 m correct to 3 significant figures
The region is a rectangle 12 m by 10 m together with two semicircles of radius 5 m.
the rectangle is 2 × 5 = 10 m wide
Rectangle: 12 × 10 = 120 m<sup>2</sup>
Two semicircles = one circle: π × 5<sup>2</sup> = 25π = 78.539… m<sup>2</sup>
Area = 199 m2 (3 s.f.)
exact value (120 + 25π) m<sup>2</sup>

items.stem: The diagram shows a sketch of triangle ABC, in which AB = 8 cm, AC = 7 cm and BC = 6 cm.

parts.t: Using a ruler and compasses only, construct triangle ABC accurately in the space below. Start by drawing the line AB of length 8 cm. Leave in all your construction arcs.
Calculate angle ACB. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.

ms:
B1 for AB = 8 cm drawn and one correct pair of arcs (radius 7 cm from A or radius 6 cm from B)
B1 for the completed triangle with both arc pairs seen, sides within ±2 mm
arcs must be seen (nfww)

M1 for cos C = 72 + 62 − 82⁄2 × 7 × 6 oe
A1 for 75.5 or 75.52…
75 or 76 alone scores M1 only
sols: Draw AB = 8 cm accurately with a ruler.
Open the compasses to 7 cm, put the point on A and draw an arc above AB.
every point of that arc is 7 cm from A
Open the compasses to 6 cm, put the point on B and draw a second arc crossing the first.
every point of that arc is 6 cm from B
The crossing point is C, because it is 7 cm from A and 6 cm from B at the same time.
Join AC and BC to complete the required triangle, leaving both arcs on the diagram.
Angle ACB is between the sides CA = 7 and CB = 6, opposite the side AB = 8.
so use the cosine rule in the ‘find an angle’ form
cos C = 72 + 62 − 82⁄2 × 7 × 6
cos C = 49 + 36 − 64⁄84 = 21⁄84 = 0.25
Angle ACB = 75.5° (1 d.p.)
it is the largest angle, opposite the longest side, so a value below 90° is reasonable here

items.stem:
The diagram shows a rectangular garden ABCD.
AB = 24 m and AD = 18 m.

parts.t: Describe fully the locus of the points inside the garden that are equidistant from AB and from AD.
Calculate the length of this locus. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

ms: The bisector of angle DAB, i.e. the straight line from A at 45° to AB

B1 for ‘the bisector of angle DAB’ oe
B1 for making clear it starts at A and ends on DC (at 45° to AB)

M1 for √(182 + 182) oe (the locus leaves the garden through DC because 18 < 24)
A1 (exact 18√2)
sols: AB and AD are two straight lines meeting at the corner A.
Points equidistant from two intersecting lines lie on the bisector of the angle between them.
Angle DAB = 90°, so the bisector makes an angle of 45° with AB.
half of the right angle at A
The locus is the bisector of angle DAB — the straight line from A at 45° to AB, ending where it meets DC.
Take A as the origin, with AB along the horizontal.
The locus is the line at 45°, so it rises 1 m for every 1 m across.
It reaches the height of DC (18 m) after travelling 18 m across, and 18 < 24, so it leaves the garden through DC, not through BC.
this is why the length uses 18 twice
Length = √(18<sup>2</sup> + 18<sup>2</sup>) = √648 = 18√2 = 25.455…
Pythagoras' theorem on a right-angled isosceles triangle
Length = 25.5 m (3 s.f.)
exact value 18√2 m

items.stem:
The diagram shows a triangular field PQR.
A well is to be dug inside the field. The well must be the same distance from PQ as from PR, and the same distance from Q as from R.

parts.t: Using a straight edge and compasses only, construct the locus of the points that are equidistant from PQ and from PR. Leave in all your construction arcs.
Using a straight edge and compasses only, construct the locus of the points that are equidistant from Q and from R, and mark the position of the well with the letter W.

ms:
B1 for correct arcs: one arc centred on P crossing PQ and PR, then two equal arcs from those crossings
B1 for the ruled bisector from P
arcs must be seen (nfww)
Perpendicular bisector of QR, with W marked

B1 for two pairs of equal arcs centred on Q and R and the ruled line through their intersections
B1 for W marked at the intersection of the two loci
FT their two constructions
sols: ‘The same distance from PQ as from PR’ means equidistant from two straight lines, so the locus is an angle bisector.
Put the compass point on P and draw one arc crossing PQ and PR.
From each crossing point, draw two arcs of equal radius that meet inside the triangle.
Rule the line from P through that meeting point — this is the bisector of angle QPR
‘The same distance from Q as from R’ means equidistant from two points, so the locus is a perpendicular bisector.
With the compasses open to more than half of QR, draw arcs from Q and equal arcs from R, above and below QR.
Rule the line through the two crossing points — the perpendicular bisector of QR.
W is where the two loci cross, since only there are both conditions true at the same time.

items.stem:
The diagram shows a rectangular park ABCD.
AB = 160 m and BC = 100 m.

parts.t: A path is built inside the park so that every point on it is the same distance from AB as it is from DC. Write down the distance of the path from AB, and the length of the path.
A dog is attached to the corner A by a lead of length 40 m. Calculate the area of the park that the dog can reach. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

ms:
B1 for 50 (m) — the path is the perpendicular bisector of AD and of BC
B1 for 160 (m)

M1 for 1⁄4 × π × 402 oe (a quarter circle, since 40 < 100 and 40 < 160)
A1 (exact 400π)
1257 also scores A1 if 1256.6… seen
sols: AB and DC are the two long sides, 100 m apart.
BC = 100 m is the distance between them
Points the same distance from both lie halfway between them.
Distance from AB = 100 ÷ 2 = 50 m
The path runs the whole way across the park, parallel to AB, so its length = 160 m
it is the same length as AB
The dog can reach every point within 40 m of A, so the boundary is an arc of a circle of radius 40 m, centre A.
The two sides at A meet at 90°, and 40 < 100 and 40 < 160, so the region is exactly a quarter circle inside the park.
the arc does not reach either B or D
Area = <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>4</sub> × π × 40<sup>2</sup> = 400π = 1256.6…
Area = 1260 m2 (3 s.f.)
exact value 400π m<sup>2</sup>

The diagram shows a rectangular courtyard PQRS, drawn to a scale of 1 cm to 4 m.
PQ = 30 m and QR = 16 m.
A statue is to be placed inside the courtyard, nearer to P than to Q and less than 10 m from SR.

parts.t: On the diagram, draw the locus of the points that are equidistant from P and from Q.
On the diagram, draw the locus of the points inside the courtyard that are 10 m from SR.
Shade the region inside the courtyard where the statue can be placed.
Calculate the area of the shaded region.

ms:
B1
a vertical line 15 m from P, i.e. the perpendicular bisector of PQ
Line parallel to SR, 10 m from it

B1
a line parallel to SR, 6 m above PQ

B1
the rectangle bounded by SP, SR, their bisector and their parallel line
FT their (a) and (b)

M1 for 15 × 10 oe, or for both correct side lengths seen
A1 cao
sols: Points equidistant from the two points P and Q lie on the perpendicular bisector of PQ.
Draw the line perpendicular to PQ through its midpoint, 15 m from P.
PQ = 30 m, so half of it is 15 m
Points 10 m from the straight line SR, inside the courtyard, form a straight line parallel to SR.
Draw the line parallel to SR, 10 m below it — that is 16 − 10 = 6 m above PQ.
‘Nearer to P than to Q’ is the side of the perpendicular bisector containing P.
‘Less than 10 m from SR’ is the side of the parallel line containing SR.
Shade the rectangle in the corner at S, bounded by SP, SR, the bisector and the parallel line.
both conditions hold there
The shaded region is a rectangle.
Its width is 15 m (from SP to the perpendicular bisector) and its height is 10 m (from SR down to the parallel line).
Area = 15 × 10 = 150 m2
Check: the whole courtyard is 30 × 16 = 480 m<sup>2</sup>, and <sup>150</sup>⁄<sub>480</sub> = 0.3125, a sensible fraction of it ✓

items.stem:
The diagram shows a rectangular exhibition hall ABCD.
AB = 40 m and BC = 24 m.
A camera at corner A can see every point of the hall that is less than 24 m from A. A second camera at corner B can see every point of the hall that is less than 15 m from B. The two shaded regions show what the cameras can see.

parts.t: Calculate the area of the hall that the camera at A can see. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
Calculate the area of the hall that the camera at B can see. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
Show that the two regions do not overlap.
Calculate the area of the hall that neither camera can see. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

ms: B1 for 24 + 15 = 39 < 40 = AB oe, with a conclusion
sols: The camera sees every point within 24 m of the corner A.
The walls AB and AD meet at 90°, and AD = BC = 24 m, so the arc just reaches D and the region is a quarter circle.
24 ≤ 24 and 24 < 40, so the quarter circle fits inside the hall
Area = <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>4</sub> × π × 24<sup>2</sup> = 144π = 452.389…
Area = 452 m2 (3 s.f.)
exact value 144π m<sup>2</sup>
The same argument applies at B, with radius 15 m.
15 < 24 and 15 < 40, so this region is also a quarter circle.
Area = <sup>1</sup>⁄<sub>4</sub> × π × 15<sup>2</sup> = 56.25π = 176.714…
Area = 177 m2 (3 s.f.)
exact value 56.25π m<sup>2</sup>
A point seen by the camera at A is less than 24 m from A; a point seen by the camera at B is less than 15 m from B.
If a point were in both regions, its distance from A plus its distance from B would be less than 24 + 15 = 39 m.
But AB = 40 m, and by the triangle inequality that sum is at least 40 m.
the shortest route from A to B is the straight line AB
39 < 40, so no point can lie in both regions — they do not overlap.
Area of the hall = 40 × 24 = 960 m<sup>2</sup>
Because the regions do not overlap, the covered area is simply 144π + 56.25π = 200.25π = 629.103… m<sup>2</sup>
Uncovered area = 960 − 629.103… = 330.896…
Area = 331 m2 (3 s.f.)
exact value (960 − 200.25π) m<sup>2</sup>
